hero.name: Sanjay
hero.who: a grape farmer near Nashik who spends his days angry at things he cannot control

story.b: Every morning Sanjay checks the weather app before he even says good morning to his wife. His three acres of grapes near Niphad are two weeks from harvest, and the sky has been grey for days. At the tea stall he complains about the clouds, the mandi rates, the traders who cheat and the buyers who never pay on time. At home he snaps at his son Omkar for leaving the tractor keys in the wrong place. At night he lies awake listing everything that could go wrong. His wife Sunanda tells him he is ruining good days by worrying about bad ones. He says she does not understand farming. But even he is tired of his own voice.

ask.q: Sanjay is exhausted by his own worry and anger. Where should he start?
o: Keep worrying, since a careful farmer must think of every danger
Separate what is truly in his hands from what is not
Blame his bad luck and wait for a better season
ask.why: Worry feels responsible, but most of his worries are about things he cannot touch, like rain and rates. Sorting what is his from what is not shows him where effort actually helps. Endless worrying wastes his energy, and blaming luck gives away the little power he does have.

chapters.take: Start by asking which part of the problem is actually yours.

story.h: Two columns on a seed packet
story.b: The forecast says unseasonal rain may come next week. Sanjay feels the familiar panic. Then, on the back of an empty seed packet, he draws two columns. In the first he writes rain, mandi rates, the trader's honesty. In the second he writes what is left: covering the weakest rows with plastic sheets, booking pickers for an early harvest, calling two more buyers, checking his crop insurance papers. The first column he cannot touch. The second keeps him busy until dark. When the rain comes on Thursday, it is lighter than feared. Some grapes split anyway. But Sanjay sleeps that night, because he did everything that was his to do.

ask.q: Omkar is stressing about whether his exam paper will be tough. What should Sanjay tell him?
o: Keep thinking about it, since worrying shows he cares
Find out from seniors exactly what will be asked
Put his energy into revision, which is his, not the paper, which is not
ask.why: The paper is set by someone else, so worrying over it changes nothing. His preparation is fully in his hands, and that is where effort pays. Worry only drains him, and chasing rumours about the questions is another way of trying to control what is not his.

chapters.take: Your effort is yours. The outcome mostly is not.

story.h: The neighbour who did not wave
story.b: On Sunday, Sanjay passes his neighbour Dattu on the village road. Dattu looks straight at him and does not wave. Sanjay's mind fills instantly. Dattu is jealous of the early harvest. Dattu thinks he is too proud. Sanjay will not invite him to the family function next month. By the time he reaches home, the story is complete. Then he catches himself. All he actually saw was a man who did not wave. Everything else was his own judgment, added on top. He decides to hold the story loosely. Two days later he hears that Dattu's father is in the district hospital, and Dattu has not slept properly in a week.

ask.q: At the mandi, a trader quotes Sanjay a low rate without even looking at his crates. What should Sanjay do first?
o: Pause, separate what happened from his judgment, then ask the trader calmly
Take it as an insult and walk away to teach him a lesson
Tell the other farmers that this trader is a cheat
ask.why: The event is a low quote without a glance. Insult and cheating are his own quick judgments. Pausing and asking calmly lets him find the real reason, perhaps a flooded market that day. Storming off or spreading a story acts on an impression he never tested.

chapters.take: Events reach you first. Your judgment of them is what upsets you.

story.b: The harvest money comes in, less than hoped but decent. His cousin Ganesh drives over in a shiny new SUV and says Sanjay should buy one too, or people will think his farm is failing. That night Sanjay lies awake wanting it. He imagines parking it outside the tea stall. Then he notices what is really pulling him. Not the car, but fear of what the tea stall thinks. A man who buys things to quiet other people's opinions is not free, whatever he drives. So he gives himself a rule: wait thirty days before any big purchase. By the fourteenth day the wanting has faded, and the money goes toward drip irrigation.

ask.q: Omkar wants expensive branded shoes because his friends will mock his old ones. What should Sanjay suggest?
o: Buy them at once so he does not feel ashamed
Notice the pull, wait a week, and ask whose opinion is really deciding
Tell his friends off so they stop mocking him
ask.why: The craving is driven by fear of other people's opinions, which are not his to control. Waiting a week and asking who is really choosing gives Omkar back the decision. Buying at once lets the mockery decide, and telling friends off tries to control them instead of his own choices.

chapters.take: Whoever controls your cravings and fears controls you. Take that power back.

story.b: Sanjay's younger brother Vilas borrowed twenty thousand rupees two years ago and has never mentioned it again. Now their mother needs cataract surgery, and Vilas says he cannot help with the cost. At a family lunch, he even jokes that farmers like Sanjay have money hidden everywhere. Sanjay feels heat rise in his face. He wants to list every rupee Vilas owes in front of everyone. Then he asks himself a quieter question. What does being a son ask of him right now? What does being an elder brother ask? The answers are clear. Make sure his mother gets her surgery. Speak to Vilas honestly, but privately, not as a show.

ask.q: Vilas is behaving unfairly about the money. How should Sanjay act as his brother?
o: Shame him in front of the family so everyone knows the truth
Stop speaking to him until he repays every rupee
Do his own part well, and raise the loan with him calmly in private
ask.why: Sanjay cannot control how Vilas behaves, but he can play his own role well. Taking care of their mother and speaking privately keeps both his duty and his dignity. Public shaming hardens Vilas, and silence punishes the whole family while changing nothing.

chapters.take: Others may play their part badly. Play yours well anyway.

story.b: Sanjay has started talking about control at the tea stall. He explains to the other farmers that rain is not theirs to worry about, and they nod politely. Then, the same evening, the power goes off during his pump timing, and he shouts at the linesman over the phone for ten minutes. Sunanda raises an eyebrow but says nothing. He gets the point. Talking was easy. Living it is another thing. So he starts small. When the bank server is down, he waits without cursing. When a neighbour's goat eats a row of his hedge, he mends the fence and lets the anger pass. He talks much less at the tea stall now.

ask.q: Omkar loves sharing wise quotes online but snaps at his sister every morning. What would Sanjay advise?
o: Practise staying calm in one small annoyance each day, starting with his sister
Share even better quotes so he keeps the ideas in mind
Wait for a big crisis to prove what he has learned
ask.why: Wisdom shows in behaviour, not in what we share or say. Small daily annoyances are the training ground where calm is built. More quotes keep it all in talk, and waiting for a big crisis means arriving untrained at the hardest test.

chapters.take: Wisdom is shown in how you act, not in what you say.

story.b: The next season, the sky over Niphad turns grey again in February. Sanjay still checks the forecast, but now he checks his two columns too. Plastic sheets are folded and ready, pickers are booked, and three buyers are on his list. He still feels the old fear, but it no longer runs his whole day. Dattu's father is home now, and the two men share tea most mornings. Vilas returned five thousand rupees last month without being asked. The drip lines are saving water and labour. At the tea stall Sanjay mostly listens. When a young farmer rants about the clouds, Sanjay asks him what he has already done about the things he can.

chapters.take: Calm comes from caring for what is yours and letting go of what is not.
